title: ORBIT: A Framework for Multi-Agent Security Evaluations
pdf_path: papers/ORBIT_A Framework for Multi-Agent Security Evaluations.pdf
threat_model_summary: Four threat classes are evaluated: indirect prompt injection, misuse, compromised agents, and collusion. Attacks use fixed payload templates; defenses include security prompting, per-action monitors, guardian agents, and dual-LLM isolation. The framework enables controlled cross-scenario comparisons but does not model an adaptive attacker.
core_contributions: ORBIT: a configurable MAS security evaluation framework built on UK AISI Inspect
Six configurable layers: setup, scenario, attack, defense, execution, evaluation
Four threat classes and four defenses across five scenario families, about 90 conditions
Controlled comparison showing per-action defenses transfer poorly from compromised agents to collusion
Monitor/guardian reduce compromised ASR from 72% to 12% but leave collusion at 30%
Documents topology effects and defense utility costs
limitations: Fixed attack payloads; no adaptive red-teaming
Attack-aware defense mapping lacks a collusion-specific criterion, confounding the collusion null result
Guardian state is per-agent, so cross-agent split vulnerabilities are structurally invisible
Customer-service is absent from the main comparison; desktop OS-Harm results are imported from a different stack
LLM judge reliability is 91%-95%; no adversarial judge test
No multiplicity correction; many cells have N=50-100
No per-defense latency/token measurements
Several internal inconsistencies in table totals and FP counts
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Byzantine/consensus work is cited as distant background, not used formally
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Dual-LLM is architectural isolation, Docker is OS isolation, and secret_channel is a simulated private channel, none cryptographic
Signed agent messages and capability gateways are our inference; they would reduce impersonation, not collusion among authenticated agents
evidence_refs: pp.5-9 framework, scenarios, and main results
pp.28-37 defense implementations and additional tables

title: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents
pdf_path: papers/Agent Meltdowns_The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: There is no adversary. Agents encounter benign local or remote errors (404, missing files, permission denied, 429) and attempt to recover; some recovery strategies overreach, subvert boundaries, or disclose data. Errors are injected singly in a Docker container.
core_contributions: Defines accidental meltdown as unsafe behavior in response to a benign environmental error without adversarial input
A taxonomy of five categories and thirteen behaviors with planned/attempted/executed/reported lifecycle and severity
A noisy-container testbed using LD_PRELOAD and MITMProxy to inject local and remote errors
64.79% of 1,920 error rollouts contain at least one medium/high behavior
78.8% of model-harness-behavior tuples exhibit some meltdown behavior
Only 50.22% of behaviors are reported; several exploration behaviors increase with model capability
limitations: No defense implemented or evaluated; results are a lower bound
Five behaviors increase with capability, but the evidence is correlational
Trace counts do not reconcile: 1,440 + 1,512 vs 1,920; 18 vs 16 model-harness tuples
Reporting rate mixes rollout-level and behavior-level denominators
Taxonomy built only from GPT-5 rollouts; other models may have unseen behaviors
Annotation validated on 260 GPT-5 behaviors, not all traces
Remote pages and emailer are simulated/mirrored, limiting external validity
No compounded or dynamically generated errors
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Contextual integrity is cited as a normative theory, not formalized
applied_crypto_links: No cryptographic mechanism is designed or evaluated
Observes TLS verification downgrade (`curl -k`, plain HTTP) and credential leakage from environment variables
Deterministic TLS verification, secret brokers, and capability gateways are our inference; they block specific behaviors but do not judge recovery intent
evidence_refs: pp.6-9 main rates, scaling, case studies
pp.24-32 appendices with traces and per-scenario tables

title: Agent MechSuits: Mechanistic Subspace Safety Steering for Multi-Turn CLI Agents
pdf_path: papers/Agent MechSuits_Mechanistic Subspace Safety Steering for Multi-Turn CLI Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious user drives a white-box open-weight CLI agent through multi-turn tasks. The defender can read hidden states and intervene at each step. Attacks are static benchmark tasks; no adaptive attacker targets the probe or steering direction.
core_contributions: Agent MechSuits: step-level linear probes on the residual stream for harmful execution detection
Top-K probe-weight-difference dimensions form a 0/1 steering vector added to all token activations
An LLM controller adaptively selects steering strength alpha without changing model weights
Current-step detection 95.35%-99.15% across three 7-9B models
Steering reduces ASR from 73.80%-92.86% to 4.35%-16.70%
A 194-task CLI multi-turn benchmark with step-level labels and counterfactual benign pairs
Negative steering demonstrates a dual-use jailbreak primitive
limitations: Requires white-box hidden states; commercial CLI agents do not expose them
Only 7-9B open-weight models, which are weak at long-horizon tasks
Static attacks; no adaptive evasion
Per-step ASR, not end-to-end task ASR
Mitigation set size is not reported; denominators may be small
ASR judge treats 'shows safety awareness' as safe even if the command still runs
Random-direction steering also reduces ASR, weakening the claimed subspace specificity
Negative steering can turn refusals into execution; no ethics/impact discussion
Internal inconsistencies in average ASR and collapse rates
theoretical_crypto_links: None; linear probes, residual-stream subspaces, and activation addition are ML interpretability methods
'Subspace' is not a lattice/code subspace; no cryptographic structure
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
TEE-protected white-box inference and signed audit logs are our inference; they protect execution and records, not the semantic safety judgment
evidence_refs: pp.16-23 appendices with implementation and ablations

title: ASPI: Seeking Ambiguity Clarification Amplifies Prompt Injection Vulnerability in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/ASPI_Seeking Ambiguity Clarification Amplifies Prompt Injection Vulnerability in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker controls environment content and can answer an agent's clarification question. The attacker cannot modify the system prompt, tools, or model weights and does not know the specific user task. The benchmark deletes one user-provided slot to force an ask_user call, then injects through the clarification response.
core_contributions: ASPI: 728 task-attack pairs across four AgentDojo domains
Deletes one required user-provided slot to create a forced clarification state
Eight conditions crossing execution/clarification with benign/tool/user/ask_user channels
Three injection operators: Hierarchy Rebinding, Goal Substitution, Constraint Poisoning
Clarification-time ASR rises to 63.1% for Kimi K2.5 and 35.7% for Gemini-3-Flash
Decomposes the headline gap into a state effect and an ask_user channel effect
Evaluates two lightweight defenses with utility costs
limitations: Synthetic single-slot, single-turn ambiguity; multi-slot and multi-turn may be worse
Depends on an explicit ask_user primitive
Single external attacker; no adaptive attacker
Only 10 models and four AgentDojo domains
Defenses evaluated on only two Gemini models
Headline state+channel comparison confounds interaction state with the ask_user channel; the isolated state effect is heterogeneous and negative for 6/10 models
Judge shares model family with evaluated agents
Several internal inconsistencies in Opus claims, utility direction, and statistical tests
theoretical_crypto_links: None; ambiguity and clarification are semantic/interaction notions, not cryptographic ones
No security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Authenticated clarification sources and task-level capabilities are our inference; they authenticate who answered, not whether the answer is malicious or contextually appropriate
evidence_refs: pp.2-8 threat model, benchmark, main results, defenses
pp.13-24 appendices with operators, prompts, tables, and judge validation

title: AgentForesight: Online Auditing for Early Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/AgentForesight_Online Auditing for Early Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: There is no adversary. A decisive error committed by one agent cascades into trajectory failure. An online auditor sees only the prefix and must either continue or raise an alarm with the responsible step and agent. Evasion and malicious agents are not modeled.
core_contributions: Reframes post-hoc failure attribution as online auditing over trajectory prefixes
AFTRAJ-2K: 2,272 trajectories, 1,158 safe and 1,114 unsafe, across coding, math, and agentic tasks
Two-stage training: BPPO on adjacent safe/unsafe prefixes, then GRPO with step/agent rewards
Exact-F1 66.44 and ASS 0.59 on AFTRAJ-2K, above DeepSeek-V4-Pro 46.56/1.77
Who&When step accuracy 57.69% and agent accuracy 73.08%
FAR 2.37% at 59.51% step accuracy; 1.03 s/call on H200
limitations: No adversarial threat model or adaptive evasion evaluation
Only predicts the decisive error; no closed-loop halt/rollback/repair
Diagnostic labels come from GPT-5.4 propose-and-verify with no human IAA
Single decisive error assumption; real failures can be multi-causal
No confidence intervals, seed variance, or significance tests
Only 332 test families
Case study Step 3 vs figure Step 5; Table 1 caption overgeneralizes zero detection
Eq. 8 threshold wording conflicts with the formula
'Early prediction' means earliest detection of an already committed error, not forecasting future failure
theoretical_crypto_links: None; online auditing is ML runtime monitoring, not cryptographic audit
No security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed audit logs and attested auditor execution are our inference; they make the verdict tamper-evident, not correct
evidence_refs: pp.2-9 definitions, training, results, case study
pp.13-29 appendices with dataset, prompts, ablations, and costs
